rows.purpose: Increase telehealth services for Individuals with Intellectual and/or Developmental Disabilities on HCBS waivers: The Division of Senior and Disabilities Services (SDS) proposes to provide access to telehealth services to more individuals receiving Home and Community Based Services (HCBS). This project will expand telehealth services to address the unique health and behavioral needs of HCBS recipients across Alaska. Currently the Division’s pilot project in telehealth services is limited to recipients of the Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (IDD) and Individualized Supports Waivers (ISW) through a contract funded with American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA) dollars that expired June 30th, 2026. This project will extend the current contract with the Division’s telehealth vendor, RingMD, and expand authorized users of this service to all individuals that receive the Adults with Physical and Developmental Disabilities (APDD) waiver. If approved, expanding access to broader waiver populations could allow Alaska to: ● Extend a proven support model to more individuals and families ● Address needs identified directly by the I/DD community ● Increase access to timely behavioral health support with clinicians specifically trained to serve individuals with intellectual and/or developmental disabilities. ● Provide additional resources for caregivers and care organizations ● Strengthen the broader disability services system ● Build on an existing platform and provider network rather than starting from scratch This expansion opportunity should be framed as a natural next step based on community demand, early clinical impact, and the platform’s demonstrated ability to support individuals during moments of need. The Alaska IDD Telehealth Platform has made meaningful progress since launch. RingMD has successfully moved the program from deployment and operational readiness into awareness, engagement, early clinical impact, and system partnership development. The platform is now demonstrating value in several important ways: ● Individuals are using it for real-time support ● Caregivers are accessing guidance and reassurance ● Providers are identifying use cases within their caseloads ● Daily and repeated use has emerged among individuals who benefit from consistent connection ● Early stage Mobile Crisis partnership work is starting to create pathways for system integration ● Community feedback suggests broader populations could benefit from similar access The program’s strongest value is that it provides a reliable, IDD-informed, supplemental support resource during moments when individuals and caregivers have limited options. It helps fill the gap between routine services and crisis response, offering timely support that can reduce escalation, improve quality of life, and strengthen continuity of care. It provides access to this valuable service in rural areas of the state that do not currently have in-person, trained clinicians for this specific population. Continued investment would allow Alaska to build on the foundation already established and move the platform into its next stage of impact: increased utilization, deeper community integration, stronger system partnerships, and expansion to an additional waiver population where awareness, trust, and utilization can translate into sustained clinical and system-level value for Alaska.

rows.purpose: Alaska Comprehensive Child Welfare Information System (CCWIS) Project: The Office of Children's Services proposes to modernize the Comprehensive Child Welfare Information System (CCWIS) . rows.purpose: Strengthening Alaska’s Correctional Health System Through Virtual Care: The Department of Corrections (DOC) proposes to implement telemedicine and teledental equipment across correctional facilities. This expansion connects incarcerated Alaskans with healthcare providers in their home communities and across the state, improving continuity of care both during incarceration and after release. Many individuals enter custody with untreated chronic medical and mental health conditions; by introducing them to telehealth services and establishing relationships with community-based providers, DOC supports smoother transitions to care upon reentry.

rows.purpose: Engaging in the Health Information System to Improve Care Coordination for Rural Alaskans: The Department of Corrections (DOC) proposes to integrate its electronic medical records with Alaska’s Health Information Exchange and Prescription Drug Monitoring Program to strengthen care transitions as individuals move between DOC and rural community providers. This will address gaps in care coordination, incomplete medical histories, and limited visibility into controlled substance use for incarcerated Alaskans across remote communities. These gaps disproportionately impact rural Alaskans, who rely heavily on continuity of care across Tribal, regional, and local health systems.

rows.purpose: Alaska Immersive Training Project: The University of Alaska Fairbanks Community and Technical College proposes to expand healthcare workforce training by deploying mobile and fixed immersive simulation systems serving rural Alaska. Immersive learning environments will provide realistic patient care scenarios and hands-on skills practice for emergency medical personnel, nurses, community health aides, and other healthcare workers in rural communities throughout Alaska.

Activities include a mixed-methods workforce needs assessment, identification of continuing education opportunities, establishment of an interdisciplinary advisory structure, and exploration of a graduate-level training pathway. The initiative addresses a critical statewide gap: Alaska has no dedicated eating disorder care and no coordinated training pathways for an estimated 65,000 Alaskans living with eating disorders.

rows.purpose: Development of an Alaska Nursing Workforce Center: AHHA proposes to incubate the Alaska Nursing Workforce Center, which would serve as Alaska's first dedicated hub for nursing workforce data, research, and strategic planning—addressing a gap as one of only four states without such a center. The project will conduct community surveys, stakeholder interviews, and facilitated engagement to identify service gaps and priorities, followed by formation of a cross-sector Community Health & Wellness Steering Committee with defined roles and measurable outcomes. Deliverables include a final assessment report and a strategic direction document to guide coordinated health investments in Nenana and surrounding communities.

The project will integrate lactation services into the primary care clinic and Cerner EMR, train additional staff to lactation consultant certification, and assess the viability of further service expansion such as home visiting. This work addresses documented postpartum care gaps for a population that must leave the community to give birth.

Without this intervention, residents of Girdwood, Hope, Whittier, Bird Creek, and Indian would face 40–90 mile trips to Anchorage for prescription medications.

The planning phase will analyze patient data to identify potential employer and insurer partners, followed by program design discussions; implementation is anticipated in the second year. The project aims to create a shared-savings APM model that reduces administrative burden, improves provider retention, and improves patient health outcomes.

Planning activities will develop operational policies, cross-agency coordination agreements with behavioral health providers and schools, workforce and training strategies, potential Medicaid billing pathways, and a phased implementation roadmap. The goal is a coordinated, treat-in-place crisis response model that reduces unnecessary emergency department use and out-of-community placements.
